intro: This is T S laws. Laws for TypeScript, checked by a compiler, a prover, and a real browser.
what: When an agent writes your code, the hard question is, how do you know it is right? T S laws answers it. You, the person, write laws: short statements about what your code must always do. The agent writes the code. And every change is checked against your laws before it lands.
basic: Here is a small project with five laws. T S laws is checking them now. Each law is proved with the Z3 solver when it can be, and tested with generated inputs when it cannot.
fails: One law fails. The sort function drops duplicate numbers.
shrunk: The counterexample is shrunk to the smallest input that breaks the law, with a seed to reproduce it. An agent gets exactly what it needs to fix the code, and a person can read why.
how: This is the law itself. A law is part of the language. You write the word law, a name, typed parameters, and a body that returns true. The compiler, a fork of the TypeScript compiler, understands it and checks it like any other declaration. It is still full TypeScript, with no restricted subset.
proved: This law is proved. A Z3 proof says it holds for every number, not just a sample.
tested: This one is tested: a couple of hundred generated inputs, and a recorded seed to replay any failure.
lock: Laws belong to people. An agent can propose laws, but only a person can accept them, in a terminal. A lock file records every accepted law, so if an agent quietly edits one to make its code pass, the check reports it as tampered.
react: Now a React app. Laws can run inside a real browser, at the component level, with any framework or none.
all: Component, accessibility, speed and model laws all report in one dashboard.
a11y: Accessibility: axe core audits the real rendered board, for every generated state.
speed: Speed: adding a task has a time budget, measured in the browser, on boards of up to two hundred tasks.
block: And it must not block the main thread. Long tasks are measured in the page.
rerun: Run everything again, and watch the real page under test, live, while each law runs.
watch: Edit a file, and the laws rerun on their own.
e2e: For a whole app, end to end laws start the real server and drive the page in a real browser.
e2erun: This law adds tasks and ticks some off, and the counter must always match. The same run checks the whole page for accessibility, and for load speed against a budget.
more: And there is more. Mutation testing checks that your laws really catch bugs. Failures are remembered and replayed first, so a fixed bug stays fixed. Results go to C I in text, JSON, JUnit and GitHub formats. There is a V S Code extension, and a server that agents can call directly.
benefits: The benefits. You can trust code you did not write. Every bug comes with the smallest example that breaks it. Where it can, T S laws gives proof, not just tests. Agents cannot quietly weaken your rules. And you stay in TypeScript.
outro: Install it with npm i dash D T S laws, run T S laws init, and write your first law.
